pending_articles.title: Information coding strategies in biological reservoir computing for multiclass time-series classification
pending_articles.content: Physical reservoir computing (RC) using biological neural networks (BNNs) offers a framework for probing how high-dimensional dynamics arising from multicellular systems support complex information processing in the brain. However, how electrical inputs and extracellular readouts should be designed to suit different task demands remains unclear. Here, using primary rat cortical neurons cultured on a high-density microelectrode array, we investigated how input encoding and spike detection methods influence neural representations and the resulting RC performance in BNNs. Comparison of pulse amplitude modulation and latency coding revealed that the latter exhibited superior performance in demanding multiclass conditions, including a 10% improvement in a 10-class spoken digit classification task. Spike sorting further improved classification performance by enhancing class separability, while largely preserving the low-dimensional structure of population activity. These findings highlight the importance of designing information coding strategies according to task difficulty.
pending_articles.author: Nishi, Y., Yamamoto, H., Katori, Y., Sato, S.

pending_articles.title: Focal neuronal loss and cell replacement in a connectome model of fly steering
pending_articles.content: Focal neuronal loss after stroke, traumatic brain injury or spinal cord injury can disrupt circuits and result in persistent motor deficits. Which cells and connections must be restored to recover a specific behavior is difficult to establish experimentally. Here we use a connectome-constrained spiking model of the fruit-fly nervous system and decode motor-neuron output to simulate visually guided steering. After loss of 4,000 neurons, path straightness ranged from 0.04 to 0.95 depending on lesion location. At a fixed sensorimotor site, a 2,000-neuron lesion reduced simulated displacement to 6.5% of intact. Across 100 stochastic simulation realizations of the connectome, replacing 100 cells with their original connections increased displacement to 62.5% of intact when motor-control pathways were prioritized, compared with 10.1% after random selection of 100 cells and 48.5% after random selection of 1,000 cells. When connections were instead inferred from cell type, the same 100 intended replacements reached 60.0% of intact with matched identities and 6.7% with non-target identities, indicating that cell identity and type-dependent integration are required for recovery. Our model generates testable predictions for genetic ablation experiments in fruit flies and identifies candidate cellular and circuit requirements for motor repair that can inform cell replacement therapies and future models of mammalian locomotion.
pending_articles.author: Habib, P., Petr, M., Rust, R.

pending_articles.title: A canonical input to the head direction compass carries predominantly eye movement signals
pending_articles.content: The mammalian head direction (HD) system is thought to update its internal compass using angular head velocity (AHV) signals relayed from the brainstem. We tested this canonical interpretation by recording from the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi (NPH), a proposed AHV relay known to be important for accurate HD tracking, while simultaneously measuring eye and head movements in mice. Neurons classified as AHV-tuned instead predominantly encoded eye movements: most showed saccade-related bursts or pauses, and apparent AHV tuning was largely explained by eye rather than head motion. Optotagging showed that even NPH neurons projecting directly to the HD circuit predominantly encoded eye movements. Empirically constrained population models reconstructed eye position and gaze direction, but head-direction readouts failed when eye and head motion were dissociated. These findings overturn the canonical view of NPH as a dedicated AHV relay, revealing eye movements as a major, previously unmeasured component of the signals entering the mammalian HD circuit and thereby changing the computational problem that the HD system must solve to maintain a stable representation of heading.
pending_articles.author: Stott, J. J., Chang, H. H. V., Bao, C., Zhang, K., Cullen, K. E., van der Meer, M. A.

pending_articles.title: High-content imaging of live microglia-containing Alzheimer's disease brain organoids
pending_articles.content: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common progressive neurodegenerative disease for which there is currently no safe and effective treatment. AD is characterized by the pathological aggregation of amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) in the brain resulting in neuronal dysfunction/death and cognitive decline. Modeling these processes in vitro remains challenging due to the lack of an immune-competent 3D in vitro human model of AD amenable to high-throughput analyses. Conventional cerebral organoids (COs) lack microglia and are optically dense which precludes real-time longitudinal analyses. Here, we employ the fluorescent amyloid probe PyrPeg to selectively monitor A{beta} aggregation, and calcein AM and propidium iodide to assess cellular viability within microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We identify age-dependent DS-AD-associated phenotypes within T21 MCOs including A{beta} neuropathology, neurodegeneration, and glial cell dysregulation. Our platform supports real-time, multiplexed tracking of disease progression and provides a scalable platform for longitudinal analyses studying disease mechanisms and targeted approaches to treatment.
pending_articles.author: Quang, D., Summers, R., Dooling, B. R., Esquer, H., Zhou, Q., LaBarbera, D. V., Vergara, M. N., Chial, H. J., Potter, H., Johnson, N. R.

pending_articles.title: Scalp EEG detects motor sequence replay signatures during wakeful rest
pending_articles.content: Brief wakeful rest may support motor-memory processing through replay of recently practiced neural sequences, but human motor replay has been demonstrated mainly with invasive recordings or magnetoencephalography. Here we tested whether ordered motor-sequence replay can be detected from scalp EEG across wakeful rest during motor skill learning. During rest, participants received no cue, regular or accelerated auditory targeted-memory reactivation (TMR), or randomized tones. Neural states re-emerged in the practiced sequence order, revealing forward replay across conditions. Accelerated TMR enhanced total learning; within this condition, stronger forward replay showed the clearest exploratory relationship with micro-offline gains, while forward and reverse replay also covaried with gains across the cohort. The apparent replay timescale shifted systematically with decoder temporal resolution, showing that measured timing reflects both neural dynamics and the observation model. These findings support scalp EEG as a scalable approach for studying ordered motor-sequence reactivation during wakeful rest.
pending_articles.author: Dash, D., Sugata, H.

pending_articles.title: Auditory tracking magnitude, temporal alignment, and anatomical distribution during wakefulness and propofol-based anesthesia in human sEEG
pending_articles.content: General anesthesia attenuates auditory responses, but response magnitude alone does not describe how residual activity aligns with sound over time or varies across the brain. We jointly characterized these aspects of auditory tracking using stereoelectroencephalography (sEEG) in 13 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy during wakefulness and clinically defined unresponsiveness under propofol-based anesthesia. The same rhythmic humming sequences were presented at approximately 1.61 Hz in both sessions. During anesthesia, stimulus-rate power showed widespread reductions and phase alignment with the stimulus rhythm was less consistent, although responses remained detectable at some recording channels. During wakefulness, response strength decreased with cortical surface distance from posteromedial Heschl's gyrus; this distance-response relationship was weaker during anesthesia. In a contrastive learning analysis (CEBRA), low-dimensional embeddings derived from anesthesia recordings yielded lower acoustic-envelope decoding accuracy on held-out data and lower consistency across model fits. Together, these findings characterize how attenuated auditory tracking is expressed jointly in response magnitude, temporal alignment, and anatomical distribution.

recently_processed.title: Neurotransmitter receptor architecture links local neurochemistry to semantic memory
recently_processed.content: A fundamental challenge in neuroscience is understanding how the molecular and neurochemical architecture of the human cortex gives rise to sophisticated higher cognitive functions. The anterior temporal lobe (ATL) is a key hub for semantic memory, and its underlying GABAergic and glutamatergic neurochemistry supports semantic memory performance. However, the molecular receptor architecture underlying these neurochemical-cognitive relationships remains unknown. Here, we combined imaging transcriptomics and in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) to investigate how neurotransmitter receptor organisation relates to local neurochemistry and semantic memory in the human ATL. We found that the ATL exhibited a distinct transcriptomically inferred receptor-subunit profile relative to control cortical regions (occipital cortex and vertex). Individual-specific spatial estimates of receptor-subunit gene expression were systematically associated with local GABA+ and Glx concentrations, revealing preferential coupling between GABAergic receptor genes and GABA+ and between glutamatergic receptor genes and Glx, alongside widespread cross-system associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and Glx. ATL GABA+ and Glx concentrations were positively associated with semantic memory performance, and GABAergic and glutamatergic receptor-subunit expression showed selective relationships with semantic memory accuracy. Crucially, mediation analyses revealed that GABA+ mediated associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and semantic performance, whereas Glx mediated both glutamatergic and widespread GABAergic receptor associations. Together, these findings reveal a coupled molecular-neurochemical architecture of the human ATL, linking neurotransmitter receptor organisation to regional neurochemical state and individual differences in semantic memory. Our findings provide a multiscale account of how cortical molecular organisation is associated with human higher cognitive function.
recently_processed.author: Jung, J., Gim, J.-A., Lambon Ralph, M.

recently_processed.title: Heterogeneous plasticity rules generate diverse structures in recurrent networks
recently_processed.content: How do local changes at individual synapses give rise to structured recurrent connectivity? Experiments have revealed diverse forms of spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) across the brain, making it difficult to predict which circuit structures different rules will generate. We developed an analytical framework mapping excitatory Hebbian, anti-Hebbian, and symmetric STDP rules to directed three-neuron motifs. Individual homogeneous rules generate restricted subsets of motifs, and no single rule produces all motifs. Combining different rules generates motifs inaccessible to individual rules and yields the full motif repertoire, and these predictions generalize to larger recurrent networks. The mapping is nevertheless highly non-unique, with distinct rules and parameters producing similar motif distributions, including distributions compatible with experimental connectivity. Thus, circuit structure constrains candidate plasticity rules but does not uniquely identify them. Finally, networks with similar motif distributions can nonetheless differ in their firing rates and pairwise correlations, suggesting that activity may provide an additional constraint on candidate plasticity rules.
recently_processed.author: Cusseddu, C., Festa, D., Miehl, C., Gjorgjieva, J.

recently_processed.title: Cerebello-basal ganglia networks and behavior across adulthood and aging
recently_processed.content: The cerebellum contributes to aging, cognition, and reward related processing, but has been relatively understudied in these domains. The cerebello-basal ganglia (CB-BG) circuit may be key to better understanding how the brain ages. Prior work has implicated this circuit in aging in a small sample, though it is also of interest in age-related neurodegenerative disease, particularly Parkinson's Disease. Here, we investigated the CB-BG network, which has been implicated in modulation of cognitive, motor, and reward-related functions. In a sample of 138 participants between the ages of 35 and 86 we looked at network connectivity in cognitive and motor sub-circuits. Participants completed motor and cognitive testing batteries followed by 26 minutes of resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI). This data was analyzed using the CONN toolbox with an ROI-ROI approach targeting the CB-BG circuit. We replicated the previously mapped cognitive subcircuit and motor subcircuits. When examining connectivity by age group (early and late middle age and older adult hood), we found higher functional connectivity in early middle age compared to older adulthood, with no results related to late middle age. Analysis of connectivity as it relates to performance on the Stroop task showed higher connectivity-behavior associations in early middle-aged adults compared to older adults. We also explored sex differences and found higher functional connectivity in females compared to males. Analysis of steroid hormone levels revealed higher connectivity associated with progesterone in females relative to males. Together, we have replicated motor and cognitive CB-BG subcircuits and further demonstrated that this network has altered connectivity associated with age, sex, progesterone, and cognitive performance. This expanded investigation of CB-BG networks represents an essential new step in increasing our knowledge of age-related cognitive and motor declines and may be particularly relevant for consideration in Parkinson's Disease.
recently_processed.author: Delaney, C., Herrejon, I., Magalhaes, T. N. C., Jackson, T. B., Hicks, T. H., Bernard, J. A.

recently_processed.title: Ms4a4a loss preferentially remodels microglia with limited, compartment-specific effects across central and peripheral immune compartments in 5xFAD mice
recently_processed.content: Background: Genome-wide association studies have identified the MS4A locus as a major modifier of Alzheimers disease (AD) risk and resilience. MS4A4A is enriched in microglia, and we previously demonstrated that loss of Ms4a4a reduces amyloid plaque pathology and attenuates amyloid-associated tau spreading. However, MS4A4A is also expressed in peripheral myeloid populations, raising the possibility that its effects extend beyond brain-resident microglia. Here, we sought to define how constitutive Ms4a4a loss alters immune populations across central nervous system (CNS), CNS-border, and peripheral compartments in the context of amyloid pathology. Methods: We performed multicompartment immune profiling by flow cytometry in 5xFAD Ms4a4a wild-type and 5xFAD Ms4a4a-deficient mice. Myeloid and lymphoid populations were characterized in the brain, dural meninges, skull bone marrow, tibial bone marrow, and spleen. Results: Ms4a4a loss produced its strongest immune effects in brain microglia. 5xFAD Ms4a4a-deficient mice exhibited increased microglial abundance, increased frequency and expression of CD86, increased MHC class II expression intensity, and enrichment of CXCR4-high microglia, whereas P2RY12 and TREM2 were unchanged. Brain macrophages showed increased MHC class II expression, whereas conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) in the brain showed reduced MHC class II expression, with limited changes in other infiltrating immune populations. Immune composition in the dura and skull bone marrow was largely preserved, although MHC class II expression was increased in skull bone marrow cDCs. Peripheral immune composition in tibial bone marrow and spleen was similarly preserved, with selective increases in M2-like macrophages in tibial bone marrow and splenic CD8 T-cell frequency. Conclusions: These findings identify microglia as the immune population most strongly remodeled by Ms4a4a loss in the setting of amyloid pathology. Constitutive Ms4a4a deficiency does not produce broad systemic immune remodeling but instead preferentially alters microglial state, accompanied by more limited, cell type- and tissue-specific effects across other central and peripheral immune compartments. These findings establish MS4A4A as a context-dependent regulator of immune responses to AD pathology with particularly prominent effects on microglia.

recently_processed.title: New Paper: Does the P3b component reflect working memory updating?
recently_processed.content:
Carrasco, C. D., Simmons, A. M., Kiat, J. E., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Enhanced working memory representations for rare events. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.70038 [preprint]

For decades, many ERP researchers have believed that the P3b wave (sometimes called P300) is a scalp manifestation of a process that updates working memory. This idea originated with Manny Donchin’s context updating hypothesis of the P3b (Donchin, 1981). Donchin’s idea of context was pretty different from working memory, but as this hypothesis percolated through the field over time, it gradually morphed into the idea that the P3b reflects the updating of working memory.

Rolf Verleger mounted a major attack on the original context updating hypothesis in a classic review article in BBS (Verleger, 1988), which was followed by a vigorous rebuttal by Donchin and Coles (1988). These are interesting papers to read, but they did not settle the issue. In the ensuing years, as the field became more focused on working memory instead of context, I’m aware of no studies that directly tested the hypothesis that the P3b reflects working memory updating.

One reason for the lack of direct evidence is that the oddball paradigms typically used to elicit the P3b do not provide a sensitive assessment of working memory. In a typical paradigm, for example, participants would see a sequence of 90% Xs and 10% Os, and the task would be to press one button for X and another button for O. The responses are made immediately, so it is not necessary to store the stimuli in working memory. Even if participants were asked to make a delayed response, the Xs and Os are so easily discriminable that memory performance would likely be at ceiling.

A few years ago, my lab (especially Carlos Carrasco, Aaron Simmons, and John Kiat) got interested in trying to test the working memory encoding hypothesis. We ran a couple of experiments, but we couldn’t quite figure out the right design. Finally, we figured it out. We used a modified oddball paradigm in which a little dot appeared at one of many locations around an circle (see Figure 1).

On each trial, participants pressed one button if the circle was close to one of the four cardinal axes (left, right, top, and bottom) and a different button if it was close to one of the four diagonals (upper left, upper right, lower left, and lower right). One of these two categories was rare (the oddballs) and the other was frequent (the standards; counterbalanced across trial blocks). As is usual in oddball paradigms, the P3b was much larger for trials in the rare category than for trials in the frequent category (see Figure 2).

The main question was whether the location of the dot was encoded in working memory better for the oddball trials than for the standard trials. To assess this, the experimental design contained occasional probe trials on which participants used the mouse to click on the exact location of the dot (see Figure 3). That is, after participants made the cardinal/diagonal buttonpress responses, they were sometimes then asked to click on the remembered location of the dot. This happened on only 12.5% of trials, selected at random, so that participants would mainly focus on the oddball task.

We looked at the accuracy of these probe responses, calculated as the (absolute value of the) angular distance between the true location and the reported location. As shown in Figure 4, the response error of the probe responses was reduced for the oddball trials relative to the standard trials. In other words, working memory was better for the P3b-eliciting oddball trials than for the standards. Moreover, we found that participants with large P3b amplitudes on oddball trials had smaller response errors on oddball trials (whereas this correlation was not present for standards).

At first glance, these findings seem like support for the idea that the P3b reflects working memory updating. However, the story is not that simple. For example, when we looked at single-trial P3b amplitudes, response errors were not lower for trials with larger P3b amplitudes than for trials with smaller P3b amplitudes.

We also used ERP decoding to test whether the exact location of the dot was better stored in working memory on oddball trials than on standard trials (click here for information about how ERP decoding works and how you can decode your own data using ERPLAB Toolbox). As shown in Figure 5, we could decode the location of the dot better on oddball trials than on standard trials during the period following the P3b component. Note, however, that this was a pretty small difference that only barely crossed the threshold for statistical significance (p = .048). I would really like to see this effect replicated before fully believing it. However, the behavioral effect was rock solid (and replicated in a follow-up experiment).

What can we conclude from these findings? When we started the project, I knew that it would be difficult to draw any strong causal conclusions about the relationship between the P3b component and working memory updating. That is, even if we saw both a larger P3b and improved working memory on oddball trials, this would just be a correlation and could potentially be explained by a third variable such as attention. But if we saw a big difference in working memory between oddballs and standards, and if we found that working memory was better on trials with larger P3b amplitudes, this would be at least consistent with the idea that the process that produces the P3b on the scalp is also involved in working memory encoding.

However, although we saw an enormous difference in P3b amplitude between oddball trials and standard trials, we saw only small differences in working memory between oddballs and standards, whether measured via behavioral response errors on probe trials or EEG decoding accuracy. If the process that generates the scalp P3b voltage plays a major role in working memory encoding, then we would have expected a much larger working memory difference between oddballs and standards. Moreover, although we found that participants with larger P3b amplitudes had smaller response errors, we did not find any evidence that working memory was any better on trials with larger P3b amplitudes (even though we looked very hard for such a relationship). The bottom line is that, although I was really hoping we would finally provide some direct evidence for the working memory encoding hypothesis, the results of this study have actually convinced me that the P3b is probably not related to working memory encoding.

What, then, explains the small but statistically significant differences in working memory accuracy between oddballs and standards, along with the subjectwise correlation between P3b amplitude and behavioral response errors? A very plausible explanation is that both the P3b component and working memory encoding are facilitated by increased attention. That is, there are several sources of evidence that rare events trigger increased attention, and this could independently produce a larger P3b and improved working memory.

Of course, this is just one experiment, so I wouldn’t say that the working memory encoding hypothesis is completely dead. But given our new findings and the general lack of direct evidence for the hypothesis, it’s on life support.

If the P3b doesn’t reflect working memory encoding, then what does it reflect? This seems like a significant question: the P3b is huge and is observed across a broad range of experimental paradigms, and it’s reasonable to assume that the underlying process must be important for the brain to devote so many watts of energy to it. In fact, I find it embarrassing that our field has not answered this question in the 60 years since the P3b was first discovered.

My best bet is that the P3b is related to the process of making decisions about actions (where the term actions is broadly construed to include the withholding of responses and mental actions such as counting). This is related to the fact that the amplitude of the P3b is related to the probability of a task-defined category, not the probability of a physical stimulus category. Rolf Verleger has a nice review of the evidence for this idea (Verleger, 2020). But it is still not clear to me why the brain devotes so many watts of energy to creating a large P3b when a rare task-defined category occurs. Verleger notes that several hypotheses about the P3b are compatible with the finding of a larger P3b for oddballs than for standards, but in my view these hypotheses have a hard time explaining the enormous size of the P3b observed for oddballs. This is a longstanding mystery in need of a solution!
